«ἔκτισά μοι υἱόν» ἢ ὁ υἱός·
english: Again, regarding the Colossians and the Hebrews, it is written: 'who is the image of the invisible God' (Col 1:15). And in the Gospel according to John, the Son, presenting his own essence to be stamped with a Fatherly character, said: 'for this God the Father has stamped' (John 5:23).

This makes manifest the co-existence of the seal with the archetype, being of like-nature, and in itself showing perfectly and truly the unity of nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the seal, just like the character, signifies that which is similar and undefiled.

Since it is a time to speak, and it is not improper or incomparable to have the Father [as the archetype], even if he is being imaged and characterized by a created and dissimilar thing. These divine things, not understanding correctly the words of unsearchable interpretation, but twisting them and contending with human thoughts against the words of God, say: 'another God and another image of God, just as another man and another image of a man.'

And in a certain way they represent the living and active God-Logos as a motionless image. But in essence and in every respect, he is an unerring and sovereign image of the Father, and not according to form and shape, like a statue carved or sculpted, breathless and not self-moving, nor according to kind and color, like an artificial and imitative silent image. For these things do not even according to nature, nor indeed in all other respects, manifest the Prototype.

For indeed the Son is an image of his own Father's essence of a man; but it happens to deviate in age or kind or mind or power or dignity or related things or something else. But the God-Logos unerringly and precisely images in all respects the simple, undivided, and unlike Fatherly divinity, naturally and sovereignly.

For it is not possible to think, as if he were an image of God according to something and deviates from something; nor indeed does he become an 'incomparable' image; nor is it possible through the dissimilar or the lesser or the subordinate that the true and archetypal and greater and self-determining and incomparable might be shown; nor again through the creature can the natural form of the creator be understood. For indeed no other nature demonstrates the other within itself. But even the Father is found to have become without subsistence, when the heretics do not teach the character.

Not of his hypostasis. But even the invisible, uncomposed, and formless God does not possess an image such as those they claim is imitative. And he clearly dissolves their argument and their induction, saying: 'To be equal to God was not considered a robbery.' And Moses also leads forward concerning a natural image, saying thus: 'Adam begat Seth according to his image' (Gen 5:3). Yet Seth was not necessarily of a different substance from Adam, yet he called the image and likeness of the essence an 'idea'.

But also concerning man, he says, it has been written, that he is 'an image and glory of God'. But nowhere, O you [ones], has it been written that man or any other creature is to be 'an emanation of the glory of God and a character of the hypostasis'. It is something else to be a man as an image of God, that is, the thing made of the maker, just as Solomon says concerning the product of a carpenter: 'The maker is perceived in a likeness to the things created'; but it is something else to be, according to the same form and identical and co-ruling, an emanation of glory and a character of hypostasis, in-dwelling and unerring. For he says: 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). But he who has seen a man has not seen God, just as he who has seen the product has not seen the carpenter.

But it is also necessary that for the only invisible God, that image is to be only invisible, and not the visible man according to the image. Therefore, the Son is not like any other: for he writes, 'Who shall be conformed to the Lord?' (Rom 8:29). Nor is he unlike his own Father: 'For I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), he says. And those who take the concept of the creator's image upon him, they resemble Nebuchadnezzar, worshipping an unconscious image made by [someone].

And God justly cast out Adam through the disobedience from the paradise; but the Son brought in the thief, and Adam with him, and the whole common race, as being altogether equal in divinity and goodness and lordship to the one who cast [them] out. Where has it been written that 'the Father is incomparable' to his own Only-begotten? Or that his Son is the creator and judge of all, according to his divine nature and the infinite nature of all things removed from them, is a 'creature'? Or altogether that at no time 'he was' (John 1:1)? Or where did the Father say privately, 'Create a son for me,' or the Son [say]?

φησίν, «ὁ θεὸς τῷ Μωϋσεῖ λέγων· λάλησον Ἀαρὼν καὶ τοῖς υἱοῖς αὐτοῦ· οὕτως εὐλογήσετε τὸν Ἰσραήλ·
english: "Was he created by the Father?" (16.53) Such a thing is terrible to hear and to say, and is to be avoided. 16.54 Truly, such things are found nowhere at all in the divine and spiritual scripture; on the contrary, when comparing himself to the Father, all the words concerning the divinity of the Only-begotten are found, showing him to be one with himself and of the same essence. 16.55 But no child, or infant, or offspring is ever spoken of regarding the eternal generation from above, which cannot be characterized at all, so that no one might imagine a small or subtle meaning in those previously sophistical blasphemies, but rather [he is] Son because of his perfection, his being unoriginated, and being inseparably of the same nature as the Father. 16.56 All things that are considered by some to be small regarding divinity, such as "the one who sent me is greater than I" (John 14:28) due to his philanthropic and ineffable humanity which came through us and for us, are used by the holy books. 16.57 Because of this, it is written that angels are made less, according to the apostle: "we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, through the suffering of death" (Hebrews 2:9). 16.58 I think, though I am not entirely certain, that regarding the Father and himself, he spoke showing the goodness and consubstantiality of both: "either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for from the fruit" (Matthew 12:33), he says, "the tree is known."

17.1 Since those who fight against God dare to say that those with the Son and the Holy Spirit are the first creation, while Macedonius says only the Spirit, the weight of remembering such rejected and condemned sayings would fall upon the holy and consubstantial Trinity. 17.2 We will show, setting forth the divine scriptures, how the first creation of God came to be: a first creation, exalted from the heavens, was cast down like lightning, as the Creator himself saw it well and later justly cast it down in the Gospel. 17.3 He says thus according to Job: "But behold, a beast beside you eats grass like oxen; behold, its strength is in its loins, and its power is on its belly. It set its tail like a plume..." (Job 40:15).
...his nerves are woven together, his ribs are bronze, and his back is an iron vessel. This is a beginning of a creation of the Lord made to be played with by the angels.

17.4 So he makes himself to say that the devil is a first creation, being played with by the holy angels because of his unrighteousness and the evilness of his will. But the Son, having created even this one, would not, nor indeed was the Spirit of God created.

18. Concerning the Holy Trinity and that because of the sameness of essence the same names are called on both sides of the hypostases, except for the fatherhood, sonship, and the procession of the Spirit. For this is proper to each hypostasis individually. And that at times the Father, at times the Son, at times the Spirit will be preferred. And that both the triadic and the monadic is shown in the Scripture.

18.1 Therefore, from all the things said, it has been established that those things turn out to be entirely foreign to the truth. For to find things out through cleverness is the work of sophistry, but wisdom is to investigate the Scriptures with reverence and with an appropriate reception.

18.2 It is necessary, therefore, having passed over their improbable sophistries and disputes, to wash the salty things with the intelligible water of the Holy Spirit—that is to say, to show having uncovered the ears—that the Scriptures, because of the sameness of divinity, at times name one of the divine hypostases, and at times name the three, and to each of them they similarly grant the good,

18.3 as when Moses says: 'Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one' (Deut 6:4), in order to say 'one' declaring the one divinity, but through 'Lord', then 'God' and again 'Lord' signifying the Trinity, by which all cosmic and super-cosmic good has been and will be for men; and again: 'God said, let there be an expanse, and God made the expanse, and God saw that it was good' (Gen 1:6-10); it should be noted that he also names three hypostases and names each one God, and shows the harmony and the cooperation of the one speaking, the one making, and the one praising.
18.4 And again: 'God stands as protector,' he says, 'speaking to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons: thus you shall bless Israel;...'

english: “May the Lord bless you and keep you, may the Lord make his face shine upon you and have mercy on you, may the Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace.” (Numbers 6:24-26). In order to show three persons, he did not say once: “the Lord bless you and shine upon you and give you peace,” but a third time he named [him] “Lord.”

And just as when a Persian prophet speaks divinely, bearing a voice from the person of the Father having such a saying: “Be strong, Zerubbabel, because I am with you; and my good word and my spirit are in your midst” (Zechariah 2:5); and Isaiah, saying that his mission has become similar to the similar ones of the self-existent substances, and in a few words indicating all their communion, cries out: “And now the Lord, the Lord has sent me and his spirit” (Isaiah 6:8). For he did not simply name a second time “Lord, Lord” and thus “his spirit,” but so that he might also show the substances and the one divinity and will.

And David also, for he himself rises by such a heading and makes all his songs full and proclaims, in what way he had faith according to these words: in Psalm 105: “Who is a god beside the Lord, and who is a god besides our God? The God who girds me with power”; in Psalm 70: “You are my God, the one who takes hold of me. My God, his mercy himself will come to my aid. My God will show me in my enemies”; in Psalm 95: “Sing to the Lord a new song, sing to the Lord, all the earth, sing to the Lord, bless his name”; for having named a third time either Lord or God, he demonstrated the Trinity.

But also Hannah, praying toward the kingdoms, called upon the Trinity saying: “Adonai, Lord, Eloi Sabaoth” (1 Samuel 2:1). For “Adonai” is interpreted with the Hebrew voice as “Lord”; and again with the Greek voice he said “Lord.” And a third time in Hebrew he said “Eloi Sabaoth,” which is: God of hosts, or of powers. And now also Elijah...

The Thessian, in the third history of kings, having prayed to revive the son of the Sidonian widow who was dead, breathed a third time into him and thus raised him up, showing not only through this that he himself in prayer called upon the life-giving Trinity, but also teaching us to believe and glorify no other way.
And encouraging the water-bearers to 'dip twice' and 'dip thrice', he indicated that the three highly-praised hypostases work equally and similarly everywhere in all things.

And if you wish, I will once again make known to you from a divine voice that which is moving. For in the book of Genesis, at the tower, God and Father spoke the blessed hypostases toward his own Son and his own Holy Spirit, saying: 'Come, let us descend and let us pour out their tongues there, so that each might not hear the voice of his neighbor' (Genesis 11:7).

And Moses, as I think, showing the equality of the Trinity, set forth one vine in three stocks, saying that this other stock is nowhere more advanced, so that no one might think this hypostasis to precede that one, but that we all believe the three are joined in one divinity.

For this reason also the God-breathed Scripture forbade making steps at the altar, in which the Trinity is glorified, so that the divine hypostases might not be defined as being men according to some sort of gradation.

And simply the Old Testament, bearing a type of the new, discourses mystically and in anticipation, rather alluding in many things than stating in one; and stating more than alluding to the mystery revealed later, so that it might neither strike the unhearing and not yet stable and receptive of theophany with a blunt blow, nor perhaps cause complete harm; for the one was of infinity, and the other of inhumanity. english: Through another writing the solution was provided. The new [writing] no longer speaks as in shadow and veil, but clearly and explicitly, as these testify: Paul, writing to the Romans: 'if indeed God is one' (Rom 3:30), and to the Galatians and Corinthians: 'God is one' (Gal 3:28; 1 Cor 8:6). And again to the Corinthians the second [thing]: 'the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the communion of the Holy Spirit with all of you' (1 Cor 13:13).

Here, because of the sameness of divinity, he first mentioned the Son, and so the Father, then his own Holy Spirit. And he spoke of the communion of the Holy Spirit with Father and Son of the one divinity and glory and kingship. For what other communion is there upon God? To the Ephesians: 'one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all' (Eph 4:4-6). Then to the same: 'for this reason I bend my knees to the God and Father, from whom every family is named in the heavens and on earth, so that I may give to you, according to the wealth of his glory, power to be strengthened through his own Spirit, so that the Christ may dwell in the inner man through faith in the hearts' (Eph 3:16-17).

Thus again, similarly, because of the equal dignity of the hypostases, after the Father, he first mentioned the Spirit and so the Son. And again to the Corinthians: 'I urge you also, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit, to contend with me in the prayers to God' (2 Cor 1:11).

And to the Hebrews: 'if indeed the word spoken through angels became firm, and every transgression and disobedience received just recompense, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation, which having begun to speak through the Lord, was made firm to us by those having heard, God co-testifying with signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will' (Heb 2:2-4).

Through the Lord, therefore, the Son has been revealed, and through God the Father, and then also the self-determining and almighty Holy Spirit. And the Son showed the one divinity by saying: 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God' (Mark 10:18), [and] the three equal and equal-powered [hypostases]...

The argument continues through the teaching regarding baptism. In 18.36, by not saying 'do not call me good' in a testing manner to the legalist, but asking 'why do you call me good?', he showed that he himself is good equal to the Father, and his goodness shines forth from the Father's goodness, being shown to be good having been born from the Good.

In 18.37, 'For if you know me to be good,' he says, 'do not entangle the teacher with the word' like 'Well done, good servant' (Luke 12:42), and like 'The good man brings good out of the good treasure of the heart' (Luke 6:45), and like 'Samuel was good with God and men' (1 Sam 2:26), and 'Saul, son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin, was better than all Israel by a head and above' (1 Sam 9:2), and 'The good dog lives above the dead lion' (Eccl 9:4). 'Do not withdraw from the primary Good, but recognize me as God, not another in the divinity of the Father, but in the hypostasis.'

In 18.38, for the divinity of both is one; since the first is no longer found to be a single good. 'For it was once read,' he says, 'as "It is good for you to trust in the Lord or to trust in man"' (Ps 31:23). 'For to cling to God is good.' And 'I urged you always to follow me as good and to walk after me' (Luke 9:23).

In 18.39, therefore he did not say 'No one is good except one, the Father', but 'No one is good except one, God', just as in another place he says 'Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and do not do my words?' (Luke 6:46).

In 18.40, for creation, he says, has goodness by participation, imitating, if it is permitted to say, the innate and perfect goodness of God and being saved through it. And there is an existence of that which has goodness in itself, participating in the goodness of God, clinging to Him through obedience and through love toward Him.
In 18.41, for it was written 'Those who distance themselves from you shall perish' (Ps 145:5), and 'God is far from the ungodly' (Ps 5:5), and 'Salvation is far from sinners' (Ps 34:16).
In 18.42, it is clear that this is in relation and disposition through the opposition toward the good and the degree toward virtue, but not in place.

In 18.43, since he himself is also good, being one by nature with the Good Father, he himself says in Matthew, 'Or is your eye evil because I am good?' (Matt 6:22); and again, 'Mary chose the good portion, which shall not be taken from her' (Luke 10:42). And he said 'the good portion'.

source_text: ἑαυτόν. 18.44 καὶ συνεξαγγέλλουσιν πνεύματι. ἀφανεῖς ἄνδρες, ἀλλὰ καὶ σφόδρα προσομιλήσαντες τῷ θεϊκῷ πνεύματι. 18.45 οἱ δέ εἰσιν μεταξὺ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν συνοπαδῶν αὐτοῖς οὗτοι· ὁ ἱεροψάλτης ἐν ριζʹ ψαλμῷ· «ἐξομολογεῖσθε τῷ κυρίῳ, ὅτι ἀγαθός». καὶ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ· «εἰπάτωσαν δὴ πάντες οἱ φοβούμενοι τὸν κύριον ὅτι· ἀγαθός». καὶ Ἰερεμίας ἐθρήνει· «ἀγαθὸς κύριος τοῖς ὑπομένουσιν αὐτόν, ψυχῇ ἐκζητούσῃ αὐτόν». 18.46 καὶ Ἠσαίας· «κύριος κριτὴς ἀγαθὸς τῷ οἴκῳ Ἰσραήλ». 18.47 Ὅτι δὲ καὶ τὸ ἅγιον τοῦ θεοῦ πνεῦμα ἀγαθὸν ὑπάρχει, ὁ μνημονευθεὶς ∆αυῒδ ἐν κδʹ ψαλμῷ μελῳδεῖ· «τὸ πνεῦμά σου τὸ ἀγαθὸν ὁδηγήσει με ἐν γῇ εὐθείᾳ». 18.48 πρὸς δὴ τούτοις, εἰ ἀγαθόν ἐστιν ἡ αἰώνιος ζωή, καὶ τὰ ῥήματα τοῦ υἱοῦ. ἔφη γάρ· «ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ζωή», καὶ πάλιν· «τὰ ῥήματα, ἃ λελάληκα ὑμῖν, πνεῦμά ἐστιν καὶ ζωή ἐστιν». καὶ εἰ ἀγαθὸν «τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος ὁ ἁγιασμός» καὶ ἡ ἐν τῇ φωτίσματι ἐνέργεια– συμμνημονεύεται γὰρ ὡς συνεργόν–, ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἡ διανομὴ τῶν οὐρανίων δωρημάτων, πάντως ἀγαθὸς ὁ υἱὸς καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα. 18.49 Οὐκ ἀκοῇ δὲ μόνον ἐδιδάχθημεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐθεασάμεθα, ὡς ἐγχωρεῖ, τῆς σεπτῆς καὶ ὁμοουσίου τριάδος τὸ ἰδικὸν τῶν ὑποστάσεων· 18.50 τοῦ μὲν πατρὸς ἐξ οὐρανῶν λέγοντος· «οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός», τοῦ δὲ μονογενοῦς αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ γῆς βαπτιζομένου, τοῦ δὲ ἑνὸς καὶ μόνου ἁγίου πνεύματος αὐτοῦ κατιόντος ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς καὶ μένοντος ἐπ' αὐτὸν τὸν μονογενῆ θεὸν καὶ υἱόν. 18.51 καὶ ∆αυϊτικὸν γὰρ θησαύρισμα ἐν πδʹ τοῦτο πιστοῦται ψαλμῷ, ὅτι ὁ σαρκωθεὶς ἐκ τῶν γηΐνων ἡμῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πατρὸς ἐμαρτυρεῖτο υἱός. γνώριμος δὲ πᾶσιν ὁ λόγος ἔχων ὧδε· «ἀλήθεια ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἀνέτειλεν, δικαιοσύνη ἐκ τῶν οὐρανῶν διέκυψεν». 18.52 Ὁμοίως διὰ τὸ μὴ εἶναι διαφορὰν θεότητος τῇ φρικτῇ καὶ ἀχράντῳ τριάδι ποτὲ τὸν πατέρα μετὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ ἐκφαίνουσι τὰ λόγια, ὡς ὅταν λέγῃ ∆αυῒδ μέν· «εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου· κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου», Παῦλος δέ· «χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς καὶ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ». ποτὲ δὲ τὸν πατέρα μετὰ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος συνάπτουσιν, ὡς ὅταν Ἀγγαῖος προφητεύῃ· «διότι ἐγὼ μεθ' ὑμῶν εἰμι, λέγει κύριος παντοκράτωρ, καὶ τὸ πνεῦμά μου ἐφέστηκεν ἐν μέσῳ ὑμῶν», καὶ πάλιν· «οὐκ ἐν δυνάμαι μεγάλῃ οὐδὲ ἐν ἰσχύι, ἀλλ' ἢ ἐν πνεύματί μου, εἶπεν κύριος παντοκράτωρ». 18.53 Ἐγχρονιστέον τῷ ῥητῷ. ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἔστιν ὅτε οἱ ἑτερόδοξοι, τοῦ πνεύματος σὺν τῷ πατρὶ μνημονευομένου, φασὶν ἀνυπόστατον δύναμίν τινα δηλοῦσθαι, ἠσφαλισμένως ἔχει τὸ προκείμενον ῥητόν. 18.54 Καὶ Ἠσαΐας· «καὶ νῦν κύριος ἀπέσταλκέν με καὶ τὸ 20 πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ»· καὶ πάλιν· «ἐκεῖ συνήντησαν ἔλαφοι καὶ ἔδοσαν τὰ πρόσωπα ἀλλήλων. ἀριθμῷ παρ ήλθοσαν καὶ μία αὐτῶν οὐκ ἀπώλετο. ἑτέρα τὴν ἑτέραν οὐκ ἐζήτησαν, διότι κύριος ἐνετείλατο αὐταῖς καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ συνήγαγεν αὐτάς» 18.55 Παῦλος δὲ Κορινθίοις· «οὐκ οἴδατε, ὅτι ναὸς θεοῦ ἐστε καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ οἰκεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν,» καὶ πάλιν· «ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ ἐκκέχυται ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου», καὶ πάλιν· «ἡμῖν δὲ ἀπεκάλυψεν ὁ θεὸς διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος αὐτοῦ». 18.56 Ἄλλοτε δὲ μόνον τὸν υἱὸν ὀνομάζουσιν, ὡς ἡνίκα Ἠσαΐας προφητεύῃ· «καὶ νῦν, κύριε, πατὴρ ἡμῶν σύ, ἡμεῖς δὲ πηλὸς ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν σου πάντες», Παῦλος δὲ Γαλάταις· «ὅσοι γὰρ εἰς Χριστὸν ἐβαπτίσθητε, Χριστὸν ἐνεδύσασθε». 18.57 Ἄλλοτε σὺν τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι τὸν μονογενῆ κηρύττουσιν, ὡς ὅταν Παῦλος Κορινθίοις μὲν ἐπιστέλλῃ· «ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε, ἀλλ' ἡγιάσθητε, ἀλλ' ἐδικαιώθητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἐν τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν», 18.58 Ῥωμαίοις δέ· «ἀλήθειαν λέγω ἐν Χριστῷ, οὐ ψεύδομαι, συμμαρτυρούσης μοι τῆς συνει δήσεώς μου ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ», 18.59 καὶ πάλιν· «εἰ μὲν γὰρ ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἄλλον Ἰησοῦν κηρύσσει, ὃν οὐκ ἐκηρύξαμεν, ἢ πνεῦμα ἕτερον λαμβάνετε, ὃ οὐκ ἐλάβετε». 18.60 Καὶ ἄλλοτε τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος καταμόνας ἐπιμέμνηται, ὡς ὁπόταν Ἠσαΐας μὲν προφητεύῃ· «αὐτοὶ ἠπείθησαν καὶ παρώξυναν τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον», καὶ πάλιν· «κατέβη πνεῦμα παρὰ κυρίου καὶ ὡδήγησεν αὐτούς»· 18.61 Παῦλος δὲ Κορινθίοις γράφει· «σαρκικὸς δὲ ἄνθρωπος οὐ δέχεται τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ θεοῦ». 18.62 καὶ ὣς Στέφανος ἐν ταῖς πράξεσι φάσκει· «ὑμεῖς τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ ἀντιπίπτετε», καὶ πάλιν· «ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν μάρτυρες τῶν ῥημάτων τούτων καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον» καθὰ ὡς ἐπίπαν εἰώθαμεν λέγειν· «ἡμεῖς μόνοι ἐνταῦθά ἐσμεν καὶ ὁ θεός.»
english: Himself. And they preach by the Spirit. They are not visible men, but they have conversed greatly with the divine Spirit. And these are among the others of their company: the Psalmist in a certain Psalm says: 'Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good' (Ps 106:1). And in the same: 'Let all who fear the Lord say, that He is good' (Ps 135:3). And Jeremiah lamented: 'The Lord is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul seeking Him' (Lam 3:25). And Isaiah: 'The Lord is a good judge to the house of Israel' (Isa 30:18).

Because also the Holy Spirit of God is good, the one mentioned by David in Psalm 143 sings: 'Your good Spirit shall lead me in a level land' (Ps 143:10). In addition to these, if the eternal life and the words of the Son are good—for He said: 'I am the life' (John 14:6), and again: 'The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and are life' (John 6:64)—and if the sanctification of the Holy Spirit and the energy in the illumination are good (for it is remembered as a co-worker), and also the distribution of the heavenly gifts, then the Son and the Holy Spirit are in every way good.

We were not taught by hearing alone, but we have also seen how the distinct properties of the hypostases of the incorrupt and consubstantial Trinity enter in: of the Father from heaven saying: 'This is my beloved Son' (Matt 3:17), of His Only-begotten being baptized on earth, and of His one and only Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove and remaining upon Him, the Only-begotten God and Son. For a Davidic treasure is confirmed in this Psalm, that the one incarnated from among our wombs was attested as Son by God the Father. And the word is known to all, having here: 'Truth has risen up from the earth, righteousness has bowed down from the heavens' (Ps 85:11).

Likewise, because there is no difference in deity, the words sometimes manifest the Father with the Son in the awesome and unblemished Trinity, as when David says: 'The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand' (Ps 110:1), and Paul: 'Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' (Rom 1:7). And sometimes they join the Father with the Holy Spirit, as when Haggai prophesies: 'For I am with you, says the Lord of hosts, and my Spirit has stood in the midst' (Hag 2:4).

"of you", and again: "not in great power nor in strength, but in my spirit," says the Lord Almighty (Zechariah 4:6). It must be applied to the word. For since the heretics, while the Spirit is being mentioned with the Father, claim that an unsubstantial power is being shown, the preceding word stands securely. And Isaiah: "and now the Lord has sent me and his spirit" (Isaiah 11:3); and again: "there the deer met and gave each other their faces. In number they came, and not one of them perished. The one did not seek the other, because the Lord commanded them and his spirit gathered them together" (Isaiah 65:23).

And Paul to the Corinthians: "do you not know that you are the temple of God and the spirit of God dwells in you" (1 Corinthians 3:16), and again: "the love of God is poured out in your hearts through the holy spirit" (Romans 5:5), and again: "but God has revealed to us through his spirit" (1 Corinthians 2:10). At other times they name only the Son, as when Isaiah prophesies: "and now, Lord, you are our Father, and we are all works of clay of your hands" (Isaiah 64:8); and Paul to the Galatians: "for as many as were baptized into Christ, have clothed themselves with Christ" (Galatians 3:27).

At other times they proclaim the only-begotten with the holy spirit, as when Paul writes to the Corinthians: "but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the spirit of our God" (1 Corinthians 6:11), to the Romans: "I say the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the holy spirit" (Romans 2:15), and again: "for if indeed the one coming preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or you receive another spirit, which you did not receive" (2 Corinthians 11:4).

And at other times he reminds us of the holy spirit, as when Isaiah prophesies: "they rebelled and provoked the holy spirit" (Isaiah 63:10), and again: "a spirit came down from the Lord and led them" (Isaiah 48:16); and Paul writes to the Corinthians: "but a natural man does not receive the things of the spirit of God" (1 Corinthians 2:14). And just as Stephen declares in the Acts: "you resist the holy spirit" (Acts 7:51), and again: "we are witnesses of these words and the holy spirit" (Acts 22:52), just as we have become accustomed to say: "we alone are here and God [is also]."

source_text: 18.63 καὶ ὁ σωτὴρ δὲ παρ' Ἰωάννῃ μόνου μνημονεύει τοῦ θεϊκοῦ πνεύματος λέγων· «ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ ἐκεῖνος, τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας, ὁδηγήσει ὑμᾶς εἰς τὴν ἀλήθειαν πᾶσαν». 18.64 καὶ αἱ πράξεις ὡσαύτως περὶ τούτου πιστοῦνται· «τοῦ δὲ Πέτρου διανοουμένου περὶ τοῦ ῥήματος εἶπεν αὐτῷ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον· ἀναστὰς κατάβηθι καὶ πορεύου σὺν αὐτοῖς μηδὲν διακρινόμενος, διότι ἐγὼ ἀπέσταλκα αὐτούς», καὶ πάλιν· «τάδε λέγει τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον· ἀφορίσατέ μοι τὸν Παῦλον καὶ τὸν Βαρνά βαν εἰς τὸ ἔργον, ὁ προσκέκλημαι αὐτούς». καὶ πάλιν Πέτρῳ εἶπεν τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα· «ἀναστὰς πορεύθητι» εἰς τὸν οἶκον Κορνηλίου. 18.65 καὶ αὖθις κομψευόμεναι αἱ ἀποστολικαὶ πράξεις διατριβὴν παρέχουσιν τῷ τοιῷδε λόγῳ· περιέχουσιν γάρ· «τότε ὁ Παῦλος πλησθεὶς πνεύματος ἁγίου εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτόν», καὶ ἔτι· «ὁ γὰρ Πέτρος πλησθεὶς πνεύματος ἁγίου εἶπεν πρὸς τὸν λαόν». 18.66 Σημαίνεται δὲ ὁμοίως τὸ ἰσόρροπον καὶ ἰσοδύναμον τῶν παντίμων ὑποστάσεων καὶ ἐν τῷ τὸν δεσπότην θεὸν λόγον διὰ τῆς προλεχθείσης αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸ βάπτισμα πανυμνήτου φωνῆς τὴν ἰσοτιμίαν ἑαυτῷ καὶ τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι τὴν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα φυλάξαι· 18.67 δι' ἣν αἱ ἱεραὶ βίβλοι ποτὲ μὲν πρώτου μέμνηνται τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ οὕτω τοῦ υἱοῦ ἢ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος, ποτὲ δὲ πρώτου ἐπιμέμνηνται τοῦ υἱοῦ διὰ τὸ τῆς φύσεως ἀμέριστον καὶ τῆς θεολογίας τὸ ἀδιάφορον, 18.68 ὡς ὅταν λέγῃ Ἰὼβ τρανῶς τὴν τριάδα δηλῶν· 18.68 «ζῇ κύριος, ὃς οὕτω με κέκρικεν, καὶ ὁ παντοκράτωρ ὁ πικράνας μου τὴν ψυχήν· ἦ μὴν ἔτι τῆς πνοῆς μου ἐνούσης, πνεῦμα δὲ θεῖον τὸ περιόν μοι ἐν ῥισίν». τὸ ζωοποιοῦν με ἅγιον πνεῦμά φησιν καὶ ἀναπνέειν ἔτι ποιοῦν. 18.69 καὶ ὡς ἡνίκα Παῦλος Θεσσαλονικεῦσι τὸ δεύτερον γράφει· «αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς καὶ ὁ θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ παρακαλέσει ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας», καὶ Γαλάταις· «Παῦλος ἀπόστολος οὐκ ἀπ' ἀνθρώπου οὐδὲ δι' ἀνθρώπου, ἀλλὰ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ θεοῦ πατρός», καὶ Κορινθίοις, ὡς προείρηται· «ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς καὶ ἡ κοινωνία τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος». 18.70 καὶ ὁ σωτὴρ δέ φησιν· «ἐλευσόμεθα ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ καὶ μονὴν παρ' αὐτῷ 21 ποιήσομεν». 18.71 Ποτὲ δὲ πρῶτον τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα ὀνομάζουσιν, μετέπειτα δὲ τὸν πατέρα ἢ τὸν υἱόν, ὡς ὅταν ∆αυῒδ ψάλλῃ· «ποῦ πορευθῶ ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύματός σου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ προσώπου σου ποῦ φύγω;» 18.72 καὶ ὁ Ἰὼβ τὸ εὔγνωμον δεικνὺς φάσκει· «πνεῦμα θεῖον τὸ ποιῆσάν με, πνοὴ δὲ παντοκράτορος ἡ διδάσκουσά με». 18.73 καὶ ὣς Παῦλος ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ ἐπιστολῇ Κορινθίοις γράφει· «διαιρέσεις δὲ χαρισμάτων εἰσίν, τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα· καὶ διαιρέσεις διακονι ῶν εἰσιν, ὁ δὲ αὐτὸς κύριος· καὶ διαιρέσεις ἐνεργημάτων εἰσίν, ὁ δὲ αὐτὸς θεὸς ὁ ἐνεργῶν τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν». 18.74 Ποτὲ δὲ περὶ δύο ὑποστάσεων διαλέγονται ὁμωνύμως, ὡς ὅτε Ζαχαρίας λέγει· «εἶπεν κύριος πρὸς τὸν διάβολον· ἐπιτιμήσει κύριος ἐν σοί, διάβολε». 18.75 Καὶ ἀνωτέρω ἐδείχθη διὰ πλειόνων. 19.ν Περὶ τοῦ τὸ νῦν λεχθὲν περὶ τοῦ πατρός, ἄλλοτε περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ εἰρῆσθαι ἢ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος διὰ τὸ ἐν μιᾷ θεότητι τὴν τριάδα ὑπάρχειν. 19.1 Ἐν μιᾷ τοιγαροῦν θεότητι οἱ ἱεροφάνται τὴν ἔνδοξον τριάδα ἐπιστάμενοι καὶ τὴν θεολογίαν αὐτῆς ἐπίκοινον οὖσαν, ὅπερ νῦν εἰρήκασι περὶ τοῦ πατρός, ἄλλοτε ἄλλοι περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ ἢ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος διαγορεύουσιν, οὐκ ἐναντιούμενοι ἑαυτοῖς, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ καὶ ἡμᾶς εἰδέναι τοῦτό τε αὐτὸ τῆς ὀρθῆς πίστεως τὸ καίριον· καὶ ὡς, οἵας δ' ἂν ὑποστάσεως ἐπιμνησθῶμεν ἐκ παντός, καὶ τὴν ἄλλην τῇ πίστει συνανελάβομεν, ἅτε ἀχώριστον. 19.2 ἀψευδεῖν δὲ ἀνάγκη τοὺς ἀψευδεῖς ὑποφήτας θεοῦ καὶ δόξης ἀρνουμένης τὴν ἀλήθειαν καθαροὺς τοὺς τὴν ἁπλῆν καὶ ὄντως ἀλήθειαν, τουτέστιν τὴν ἀγαθότητα, τοῦ θεοῦ διδάσκοντας. 19.3 μὴ καθαροῖς γὰρ καθαρῶν ἐφάπτεσθαι μὴ οὐχὶ θεμιτόν φασιν· οἱ δὲ ἦσαν καθαροὶ καὶ πάσης ψευδοδοξίας ἀλλότριοι. 19.4 Εὑρήσομεν δὲ τοῦτο εὐθὺς εἰς τὴν θεοπτίαν, ἣν ἐθεάσατο Ἠσαΐας. τί δὲ μὴ πρῶτον ὅλου ἐκείνου ὡς ἔχει μνημονεύσω τοῦ χωρίου; 19.5 λέγει οὖν· «εἶδον τὸν κύριον Σαβαὼθ καθήμενον ἐπὶ θρόνου ὑψηλοῦ καὶ ἐπηρμένου, καὶ πλήρης ὁ οἶκος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ. καὶ σεραφὶμ εἱστήκει σαν κύκλῳ αὐτοῦ· ἓξ πτέρυγες τῷ ἑνὶ καὶ ἓξ πτέρυγες τῷ ἑνί· καὶ ταῖς μὲν δυσὶ πτέρυξι κατεκάλυπτον τὰ πρόσωπα, ταῖς δὲ δυσὶ τοὺς πόδας, ταῖς δὲ δυσὶν ἐπέταντο· καὶ ἔκραζον ἕτερος πρὸς τὸν ἕτερον· ἅγιος ἅγιος
english: And the Savior alone mentions the divine Spirit according to John, saying: 'But when He comes, that Spirit of truth, He will guide you into all the truth' (John 16:13).

And the deeds likewise testify to this: 'And while Peter was deliberating concerning the word, the Holy Spirit said to him, Stand up, go down, and walk with them without any hesitation, because I have sent them' (Acts 10:19); and again: 'These things the Holy Spirit says: Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work, whom I have called' (Acts 13:2); and again the Holy Spirit said to Peter: 'Stand up, go' (Acts 10:33) to the house of Cornelius.

And again the apostolic deeds, being elegant, provide a demonstration by such a word; for they contain: 'Then Paul, having been filled with the Holy Spirit, said to him' (Acts 13:9), and also: 'For Peter, having been filled with the Holy Spirit, said to the people' (Acts 11:5).

Similarly, the equal-balance and equal-power of the all-divine hypostases is signified, and in the Word, the Lord God, through His most-praised voice having been foretold for the baptism, the equal-honor to Himself and to the Holy Spirit for keeping [the relation] toward the Father; through which the holy books sometimes first mention the Father and thus the Son or the Holy Spirit, and sometimes first remember the Son because of the indivisibility of nature and the indistinguishability of theology; as when Job declares the Trinity boldly: 'The Lord lives, who has thus judged me, and the Almighty, who has afflicted my soul; indeed, my breath is still remaining, but a divine spirit surrounds me in my nostrils' (Job 5:14). He says [that He is] the one making alive with a Holy Spirit and still breathing, making [it] so.

And as when Paul writes to the Thessalonians the second time: 'And our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God and Father will exhort your hearts' (1 Thess 3:11), and to the Galatians: 'Paul, an apostle, not from man nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father' (Gal 1:1), and to the Corinthians, as is previously stated: 'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and Father and the communion of the Holy Spirit' (2 Cor 13:13).
And the Savior says: 'We will come, I and the Father, and we will make a dwelling with Him alone' (John 14:21).

First they name the Holy Spirit, and then the Father or the Son, as when David sings: 'Where shall I go from your spirit, and from your face where shall I flee?' (Ps 139:7). And Job, showing his good conscience, says: 'A divine spirit made me, and the breath of the Almighty teaches me' (Job 32:8). And as Paul writes in the first epistle to the Corinthians: 'There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and diversities of operations, but the same God who works all in all' (1 Cor 12:4-6). Sometimes they speak homonymously concerning two hypostases, as when Zechariah says: 'The Lord said to the devil: The Lord will rebuke you, devil' (Zech 3:1). And it was shown more clearly through many [examples].

Concerning what has now been said about the Father, sometimes it is said about the Son or about the Holy Spirit because the Trinity exists in one divinity. In one single divinity, the hierophants, knowing the glorious Trinity and its theology being common, sometimes speak about the Father, sometimes others about the Son or about the Holy Spirit, not opposing one another, but because we also know this very thing to be the opportune part of the right faith; and just as whatever hypostasis we remember from everything, we also received the other with faith, as inseparable.

But it is necessary for the truthful ones, who deny the truth of glory, to be truthful in teaching the simple and truly true, that is, the goodness of God. For they say it is not right for the impure to touch the pure; but those were pure and strangers to all false glory. And we shall find this immediately in the theophany which Isaiah saw. And why not first [mention] the whole of that place as it is?

So he says: 'I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and the house was full of his glory. And seraphim were standing around him; six wings to the one and six wings to the one; with two wings they covered the faces, with two they covered the feet, and with two they were flying; and one was crying to another: Holy, holy' (Isa 6:1-3).

english: “Holy Lord of Sabaoth, the heaven is full of his glory and all the earth.” (Isa 6:3). He says other things: “He said to me: say to the people: by hearing you shall hear and you shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and you shall not perceive. For the heart of this people has become thick, and with their ears they have heard heavily and their eyes they have blinded, lest they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn and I might heal them.” (Isa 6:9-10). And among others he brings forward: “and the king Lord Sabaoth I saw with my eyes. And he was sent to one of the seraphim” (Isa 6:1-2) and the following.

Having seen thus the Lord Sabaoth and king, Isaiah knew that this one is God the Father (Isa 6:5). And Paul in the book of the Acts of the Apostles, finding the Holy Spirit to be, declared thus, interjecting: “The Holy Spirit spoke well to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet, saying: Go to this people and say to him: by hearing you shall hear and you shall not understand” (Acts 28:25) and the following, as it is written. And John in the Gospel distinguished the Son of God to be. For he said: “Because he has made so many signs, they were not able to believe, since Isaiah said: He has blinded their eyes and made heavy their heart, so that they might not see with their eyes and understand with their heart and turn and I might heal them” (John 2:23). And immediately he brings forward: “And Isaiah said these things when he seen his glory,” (Isa 6:1) that is, of the Son of God. These things indeed are somewhat about these matters.

But hear also other things of the same power, of David in Psalm 95, singing from the person of God the Father with the lyre thus: “Your fathers tested me and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was vexed with this generation and said: They always err in heart. But they did not know my roads. As I swore in my anger: they shall not enter into my rest” (Ps 95:7-11). Paul, writing to the Hebrews from the same psalm by the Holy Spirit, clarifies this way: “As it was said,” he says, “the Holy Spirit: Today if you hear my voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the rebellion on the day of temptation, in which your fathers tested me and saw my works for forty years” (Heb 3:7-8). And Stephen, in the Acts, spoke to the Jews from the same threatening scripture: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers and you do” (Acts 7:51). Similarly, Moses says that the Hebrews were led out of Egypt in Deuteronomy: “For the Lord,” he says, “was alone with them, and” (Deut 32:6).

english: "...and God was not a stranger among them." Jeremiah likewise says: "And you have not said, 'Where is the Lord, the one who brought you up from the land of Egypt, the one who guided you in the wilderness?'" (Jeremiah 2:19). Isaiah says that the Holy Spirit has guided: "For He led them through the deep, as a horse through the desert without tiring, and as livestock through a field, a spirit came from the Lord and guided them." (Isaiah 43:16). And Paul teaches that Christ has become their guide: "For they drank from a spiritual following rock, and the rock was Christ." (1 Corinthians 10:4). To this, Jude also writes universally: "For once the Lord Jesus, having saved a people out of Egypt, a second time destroyed those who did not believe in Him." (Jude 1:5).

There, therefore, the attempt of those who call the seventh Son and the Divine Spirit a creature is twice refuted, as is the use of 'another hypostasis' as a pretext to mark the one infinite nature as being different, and the claim that 'God was not a stranger among them,' that is to say, of a different substance. In the same manner Moses says: "There shall be no inheritance or lot for the Levites in the land; the Lord Himself is their inheritance." (Numbers 18:20). And Jeremiah says: "He who formed all things is Himself the inheritance of Jacob; the Lord is His name." (Jeremiah 10:7). And David says in the 14th Psalm: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup." (Psalm 16:5).

Paul also writes to the Ephesians that the Holy Spirit is the inheritance: "In whom," he says, "having believed, we were sealed with the Spirit of the promise, the Holy [Spirit], who is the pledge of our inheritance." (Ephesians 1:13-14). Similarly, Paul writes to the Corinthians: "There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of activities, but the same God who works all things in all." (1 Corinthians 12:4-11).

By demonstrating the identity of the Divinity, He recalls not only the Spirit first, then the Son, and thus the Father, but also, having just said that God works all things, He leads into: "And all these things works the one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to each one individually as He wills." (1 Corinthians 12:11). He clearly and explicitly presents Him as God, consubstantial with the Father and the Son at once, and as self-determining. english: 21. Concerning speaking of the Trinity through the unchangeable nature and essence in the holy ones. Speaking of equality in the holy ones announces the unchangeability of nature and the authority of the divine hypostases. For Zechariah—not the prophet, but the father of John—said that the Lord God of Israel has spoken through the prophets (Luke 1:57). And Paul similarly sent to the Hebrews: 'God, having spoken many times and in many ways of old to the fathers in the prophets, has spoken to us in this last age in His Son' (Hebrews 1:1-2). And to the Corinthians he wrote concerning the Son: 'since you seek the testing of the Christ speaking in me' (2 Corinthians 13:5). And the Savior according to Matthew teaches: 'for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father is the one speaking in you' (Matthew 10:20).

22. Concerning the fact that it is written that we live by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit through the same Word, which is the consubstantiality of the Trinity. What is written—that we live by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—teaches this to be seen most clearly; just as when Paul reasons with the Romans in letters: 'you consider yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord' (Romans 6:11). And again: 'that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for Him, Christ, who died for them and was raised up' (2 Corinthians 5:15); and to the Galatians: 'if we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit' (Galatians 5:25).

23. Concerning the fact that through this Word, the law from above is written to be of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Because of whom we said it is the Word, and the law from above is written to be of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, just as the Psalmist says in Psalm 40: 'the law of his God is in his heart,' and in Psalm 39: 'to do your will, O God, I have desired, and your law is in the midst of my womb' (Psalm 40:8; 39:8). And as Paul writes to the Galatians: 'one another's...'

english: I make known to you that no one can say 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 12:3), and again. 'But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know, because they are being judged spiritually. But the spiritual man judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one. For who has known the mind of the Lord, which directs him? But we have the mind of Christ' (1 Cor 2:14-16). And again: 'Brothers, if even a man is caught in some transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, watching yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another's burdens, and thus fulfill the law of Christ' (Gal 6:1).

Regarding the reason for the Trinity through their shared essence, what now speaks of the Father, at another time speaks of the Son or of the Holy Spirit. The Scripture, declaring one deity and lordship, now speaks of the Father, and at another time asserts that it is the Son or the Holy Spirit; just as when the uninspired Paul writes to the Philippians: 'For they all seek their own, not those of Jesus Christ' (Phil 2:21), to the Galatians: 'But those of Jesus Christ crucified the flesh with its passions and desires' (Gal 5:24), and to the Corinthians: 'For the love of Christ constrains us, judging this: that he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose for them' (2 Cor 5:14-15). And again: 'But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him' (1 Cor 2:14); and again: 'But desire the spiritual things' (1 Cor 7:40).

Furthermore, regarding the Church, which is conceived with the glory ascending within it and the bloodless worship being brought to it, writing first to the Corinthians, he announced that it belongs to God thus: 'Become without stumbling to Jews and Greeks and to the Church of God' (1 Cor 10:32), and again: 'We do not have such a custom, nor do the churches of God' (1 Cor 10:33). But writing again to the Ephesians, he taught that it is Christ's, saying thus: 'That he might present to himself the church without blemish, having no spot or wrinkle or anything of this kind, but that it might be holy and immaculate' (Eph 5:27). For since it did not seem so to him here, someone will interpret what the prophet Haggai intends by saying, 'the glory of this house shall be greater than the first' (Haggai 2:9), that is, of the Church of Christ and the glorification within it, compared to the synagogue of the Jews, in which God alone was theologized and glorified.

Therefore also the Gospel, writing to the Romans, says that it is now of God the Father: 'Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, a called apostle, set apart for the gospel of God' (Romans 1:1); and again: 'For I am not ashamed of the gospel: for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For the righteousness of God is revealed therein; and the just shall live by faith' (Romans 1:16-17); and to the Corinthians the second instance: 'that I preached to you the gospel of God freely' (1 Corinthians 2:4); but in the first instance he writes to the Corinthians that it turns out to be of the only-begotten God: 'but we have not used that authority, but we endure all things, so that we may not cut off anything by the gospel of Christ' (2 Corinthians 10:18); and the second: 'having come into Troas for the gospel of Christ' (Acts 20:7/contextual); and again: 'glorifying God in the submission of your confession unto the gospel of Christ' (2 Corinthians 10:18); and to the Romans: 'For God is my witness, whom I serve in the gospel of His Son' (Romans 15:30).

But he also said that the sacred liturgy is sometimes performed for God the Father and sometimes for God His only-begotten Son, having written to the Corinthians the first: 'Thus let a man reckon us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God; that which is required in stewards, that one be found faithful' (1 Corinthians 4:1-2); the second: 'in everything presenting ourselves as ministers of God' (2 Corinthians 4:5); and again: 'Are they ministers of Christ? I speak foolishly; rather, I do' (1 Corinthians 9:17).

english: He presents all good things as being drawn toward the one divine peace, which has no limit, about which Isaiah cried out: 'Lord our God, give us peace; for you have given us all things. Lord, besides you we know no other' (Isa 26:3). This is given by Him through His power because of the shared nature and lordship. He said: 'Peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you' (John 14:27).

Therefore, Paul also did not fail to provide this God-giving word to both the unbegotten hypostases without distinction (Rom 1:7), writing thus to the Romans: 'Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.' We are also provided the recognition of this in the same way by that: 'All that the Father has is mine' (John 16:15).

For these things are not understood ignorantly regarding creation, but are understood regarding the divine worth, if one is to say they belong to God. For the Father, he says, is God. I am also; for he is his only-begotten, true, and beloved Son. The Father is Lord. I am also lord of all and heir of the living Father, possessing the inheritance. And I inherit his own things, this as the maker of them, and this also as a genuine Son. And I was made heir as one having become man.

The Father is Creator and King. I am. For I said to you as, 'There was a king who went out to make marriages for his son the king' (Matt 22:2). The Father is unchangeable. I am also. For it has been prophesied concerning me: 'You are the same, and your years shall not fail' (Ps 70:5). The Father is impassible. I am, so as to let those who share in me partake of impassibility.

The Father is without beginning. I am. For there was not a time when the hypostatic radiance did not have the name of the Father and of his glory, and the 'character of the hypostasis' and the 'image of the deity,' which is me. Life and light and goodness and power and wisdom and truth and whatever is worthy of God, the Father is. I am, as you have heard by those who have perished.

And indeed I am also Savior, 'raising the sun upon the righteous and the sinners' (Matt 5:45) and not bringing 'evil for evil.' The Father is Philanthropic. I am, wherefore for your sake 'I emptied myself, having taken the form of a slave' (Phil 2:7), and being struck and spat upon and mocked and crucified by you.

We were not misled. All the things he said happen to be in accordance with the Fathers, so that he gives nothing more to God the Father than only being the father of a co-ruling and co-existing Son. Thus he persuades one to believe also that: 'All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine, and I have been glorified in them' (John 17:10).

For if it were not said thus through the natural relation, and if the Son had not been essentially glorified in all the Fathers, unless kingdom and lordship are one, then—according to the logic—it would be heretical, that there is something accomplished not by the authority of the Father, but by the authority of the Son. And again: 'If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me' (John 17:5).

He says, speaking about his own divine glory, that 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), do not disbelieve; rather, there is the Father witnessing for me, that according to nature I am glorified, being his beloved and true Son, yet [being] God and Lord of you. Then he says: 'Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son also may glorify you' (John 17:5). Equal honor and glory have been preserved thus for the divine hypostases. For in whatever way we conceive of the Father glorifying his Son, by that same way he himself is glorified by him.

And he proceeds again: 'And now glorify me, Father, with the glory I had with you before the world existed' (John 17:5). It is terrible to hear, that he who has glory independently from his own Father—for this is what it means: to have had glory before the world existed—is not glorified according to the heretics. And what was this [glory]? Which, as I think, Mark also said: 'When the Son comes in the glory of his Father' (Mark 8:38), instead of: he possesses the Father's glory and in it he will come a second time.

Of which glory, being one, divinity, kingdom, and worship have been established, not one and another. Therefore he commands beforehand: 'Believe in God, and believe in me. In my Father's house there are many mansions' (John 14:1-2). He says, 'that they may know one faith concerning the Trinity, not having a difference of divinity, so that you may dwell in those three-blessed courts, all in harmony and sufficiency.'
Not only, indeed, those he led, but also, providing [things] of God, he says: 'Your sins are forgiven you' (Luke 7:48). You pay attention likewise to his authority, that as if...

english: He does not act as an ambassador to a greater one, but forgives like an autocrat.

Matthew, contributing himself to the theologies concerning the only-begotten Son, said: 'No one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father' (Matt 11:27). How then do these people contend as if they knew the Father to be incomparable, his Son to be unlike him, and the essence to be unbegotten? They leave nothing exceptional in the knowledge of God the Father and the only-begotten God, nor do they consider that one who possesses nothing of a different nature possesses knowledge equal to the homoousion. Paul similarly writes to Timothy in the first epistle: 'I charge you before God who gives life to all things and Jesus Christ who bore the good confession in the presence of Pontius Pilate, to guard the unblemished command, without reproach, until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which the blessed and only powerful one and King of kings and Lord of lords, the only one having immortality and dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen or is able to see, to whom be honor and glory for the ages of ages. Amen' (1 Tim 1:17).

For it has seemed fitting to the heretics to give this to the Father alone: 'the only powerful one and King of kings' and the following. Just as regarding both of the eternal hypostases he said: 'I charge you before God and Christ Jesus,' so he sang regarding both of them as one in divinity and the following. For he did not ignore like these: 'all that the Father has is mine' (John 16:15), and: 'that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father' (John 5:23), and: 'this is the true God and eternal life' (1 John 5:20), and: 'this is our God; no other shall be reckoned against him' (Isa 42:8), and: 'this is my beloved Son' (Matt 3:17).

But rather, the things set forth are directed more toward the Son. For it says: 'to guard the command until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which the blessed and only powerful one will show in his own times.' It is clear, therefore, that the Son will show his own appearance when he comes a second time. Thus, it allows that he also grant him the first glory. To the Romans: 'for his invisible things from...'

The eternal power and divinity of the one understood through the works of the world as being created. Because of the equal value of Father and Son, it does not fall short toward a creature. For the eternity and divinity of the Creator is not to be understood in the Begotten; that is, the divinity possessing the same things always. Regarding the Philippians: 'who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be snatched, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave' (Phil 2:6).

What of this equality is found unequal? For he did not snatch, he says, he did not take to be equal in nature to God and Father. And indeed, he who was not emptied by another, but having emptied himself, simultaneously showed himself to be a Master and eternal. For if he became in the form of a slave, it is indisputable that he did not remain so, but before this happened, he was in the free paternal nature, in creatures. Since it was not possible to be seen, he descended unchangeably and invisibly until the form of a servant. english: He has the Son as greater for himself. For God having said to Abraham in Genesis, 'Bring me a sacrifice of your son' (Gen 22:2), and after he had done this willingly and was about to bring his hand upon him with a sword armed, an angel of the Lord called him, saying, 'Abraham, do not lay your hand upon the lad, nor do anything evil to him; for now I have known that you fear God and you have not withheld your only beloved son from me' (Gen 22:12).

Then, after a ram was found for the sacrifice instead of Isaac, and the sacrifice was completed by Abraham—the intention being through the boy, but the slaughter through the ram—he says, 'an angel of the Lord called him a second time from heaven, saying: I have sworn by myself, says the Lord, because you have done this thing and you have not withheld your beloved son from me; surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea; and all the nations shall be blessed in you, because you obeyed my voice' (Gen 22:16-18).

Neither the Father nor even a ministering angel was [the one swearing]. For a minister does not swear by himself, nor bless, nor say, 'I will not withhold your beloved son from me'; nor does he dare to turn away the sacrifice being brought to God, nor does he have the authority to offer it again.

But it was the only-begotten God, the Word, who sought the sacrifice, granting the only-begotten to Abraham, as Paul explains writing to the Hebrews thus: 'For God, having promised to Abraham'—which he both promised and did—'since he had nothing greater by which to swear, he swore by himself, saying: Surely blessing I will bless you' (Heb 6:13-14). And to the Romans he explains again, the one swearing by himself: 'For we shall all be presented at the judgment seat of Christ, as it is written: I live, says the Lord, that every knee shall bow to me and every tongue shall confess to God' (Rom 14:10-11). And the sitting at the right hand of the...

Yet, the Evangelist uses the term 'bosom' appearing to the Son to signify that it is the Father's bosom, unless it signifies the same and of equal nature, and that he is to be worshipped along with the Father and His Spirit, the only-begotten God and Son; but—according to human standards, for one must not receive [the words] written concerning God as if they were human—the one at the right hand is greater and more glorious than them, possessing the divine, unapproachable bosom like a many-eyed cherubic throne. May such a thing never be said regarding the most inexpressible and serene Trinity.

For David sang concerning the Father in Psalm 110: 'The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand' (Psalm 110:1). And Paul explains to the Hebrews: 'who, being the radiance of the Father's glory and the imprint of His essence, bearing all things by the word of His power, having made cleansing of sins, sat at the right hand of Majesty in the highest places' (Hebrews 1:3). And the Evangelist [says]: 'the only-begotten God who is in the bosom of the Father' (John 1:18).

Similarly, theology concerning the Son [states] that 'in Him dwells all the fullness of deity' (Colossians 2:9) and that He is 'great God' and 'over all,' 'by whom no other is counted,' 'true God,' 'eternal life,' 'sole Lord,' 'sole wonder-worker,' 'most high,' 'King,' 'Authority,' 'Christ in all in all,' and the rest. These things suffice regarding these matters; yet the mystics of the divine, desiring even more regarding the most provident Trinity, theologize about the Son just as they do about the Father, saying that 'in Him dwells all the fullness of deity' (Colossians 2:9) and that He is 'great God' and 'over all,' 'by whom no other is counted,' 'true God,' 'eternal life,' 'the true light,' 'sole Lord,' 'sole most high,' 'sole wonder-worker,' 'great King,' and 'Lord of all.'

english: "Creator" and "Ruler" and "His peace has no limit" and "Savior" and "Christ is all in all" and "Blessed forever," and that "great is the mystery of godliness," are clear; for among the Christians, Christ is praised as an unbegotten God, and that by his own divinity "he acquires the people," because he has consubstantiality with the Father.

Thus, the saints who are now to be remembered by us speak concerning these things, to whom God, according to Psalm 19, "made known the ways of life." David, in Psalm 67, prays: "Arise, O Lord my God, by command, which I have decreed, and let a gathering of peoples surround you, and return to the heights on account of this."

One perceives, as the prophet sees, that he knows the Lord and God, and he petitions him, saying "Arise" upon your unutterable becoming-human, in the manner which you foretold: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19).

For on account of this, they say, of which salvation is surrounding us: "The nations shall surround you by faith; and you, from whence you came, shall return unseparatedly"; and in Psalm 45: "Great God, Lord, and great King over all the earth." And in Psalm 44: "From the risings of the sun even to the settings, the splendor of his beauty is from Zion; God shall come visibly"; and in Psalm 67: "Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered," and "Make way for him who has set foot toward the west; Lord is his name"; and in Psalm 69: "Arise, O God, judge the earth."

Behold, how each word lifts up the glory concerning him and suffices to persuade that he exists as the essence of the Father's unity; and that the great writer calls God he who was placed in the tomb not without life, so that he might save both the living and those departed from human affairs, and he prophesies rising, judging those who have thought wisely regarding so much and such a great blessing.
Know, however, that "the west" refers to the last times; for in them this spectacle has visibly appeared to this world.

And in Psalm 69: "In the holy is your way. Who is a great God like our God? You are the God who does wonders alone." Here the incarnate God-Word is praised without words, he who entered into the Jewish temple and taught and worked wonders.

english: Lord: 'you alone are most high over all the earth' (Psalm 53:6), saying 'alone' because of the one divinity. He called him Father of eternity, being the creator of even the past ages, because he was known by men much more through the temporal aspect of the economy.

Therefore, he called him Father, as a creator and not of uncreated nature; for one is the Father of the uncreated and consubstantial Son. And to demonstrate his divinity, he said something simple: 'there is no limit to his peace.'

And Jeremiah, or rather, for the book of Baruch is one of both, solemnly speaks about him: 'This is our God; no other shall be reckoned against him (Isaiah 42:8). He found every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his child and to Israel, the one beloved by him; after these things he appeared upon the earth and walked among men.'

If, therefore, it is not conceived in a God-befitting manner that the present scripture was spoken thus because of the shared divinity of both the unutterable hypostases, it remains to say, effectively blaspheming, that the one who created is God and Father, but not our God, and is not comparable to his Son.

Thus, the word of those who slander has fallen away and spread, making the God the Word smaller and a subordinate. For how could another be incomparable to God, 'to whom no other shall be reckoned against him'?

And again: 'gods, who did not make heaven and earth, destroyed upon the earth; Lord, who made the heavens in wisdom, he is the living and true God' (Psalm 95:3), as if there were another divinity that is not true, except that of the genuine Son of God, through whom and from whom and by whom the heavens were also provided for the whole world.

And Paul, the preeminent of men, following the same sequence, gives words fittingly concerning him, writing to Titus: 'awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, to redeem us from all lawlessness and to cleanse for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works' (Titus 2:13).

For through the being called 'the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ,' it is made manifest that he does not have a second-rank status in essence, and [the distinction] of the unoriginate toward the great God the Father.

For according to appearances it is possible to conclude that if the Son is small, how will the Father be great? If the Word God 'was when he was not' (John 1:1), he was when the name of the Father did not exist. Let it be gracious to us that we dare to say such things because of the ignorance of others. 'For piety is a beautiful habit', they say, 'for those using it'.

But through the saying 'of the one giving himself for us, in order that he might cleanse for himself a people of his own possession' (Hebrews 5:9)—not for another in order that he might cleanse a people—it follows what has been mentioned. For it signifies that he himself, the one single, self-possessing and good deity, who is the cause of all, has been determined. For it is a peculiar thing for a creator, indeed, not to surpass his own creation, if it must be said so of his own work; but for the deity of a beloved Son, having no difference from the Father, to acquire the people for himself.

And this great and true interpreter leads the argument to demonstrate that he is at once a philanthropic Savior God, and at once, as he himself veiled himself and did not show himself as superior in deity, to become with us as one of us, through a change and through sin, he asserts: 'When indeed the kindness and the philanthropy of our Savior God appeared, not because of the works which we ourselves did, but according to his great mercy, he saved us through the bath of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit'.

And he also reproaches the Colossians and makes a disparagement of the primary theology concerning him by the writings, as it has already been said in the chapter 'on the consubstantial': 'Why according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ Jesus? For in him dwells all the fullness of deity bodily' (Colossians 2:9), that is, essentially. For he also is by nature a fullness, the Father's deity existing in essence.

For 'being equal to God was not considered a robbery' (Philippians 2:6); but we received from the fullness because of his goodness. Which we by nature as slaves did not have, John saying: 'And from his fullness we all have received, and grace for grace' (John 1:16), that is, the grace of the rebirth instead of the grace which we were cast away from, striking at the first law given upon the single stock. english: He says, 'you are under law, but under grace' (Rom 6:14); and again, 'because in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell and through him to reconcile all things to himself' (Col 1:19-20).

These things follow the previous ones. For the Father being in the Son and the Son in the Father by nature, just as every relative is inseparable as he becomes of his own kin, even if he is divided by subsistence, the argument on the moving ground is good, even if not very deeply, but not to all clearly: 'through him and to him to reconcile all things' (Col 1:20), as it is fitting to harmonize the Son with that which was said concerning the Father: 'from whom all things' (Rom 5:17), if what has been said now and then is held soundly; 'in whom dwells all the fullness of deity' (Col 2:9).

And having written to Timothy, he theologized about him to the end, and from both sets of words he taught that the Father is not according to deity by nature. For he said such as this: 'unquestionably great is the mystery of piety: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the Gentiles, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory' (1 Tim 3:16).

For this creator and benefactor of all things was not yet clearly manifest to all, when he became willing through the salvation of all and as one of all. Therefore, 'was justified in the spirit,' that is, he was shown or confirmed even by those who had ignored him in later time to be a true God; and this, he says, is not without reason, but by that movement of our soul, as common custom has it to say: 'he who was thus justified was truly the Son of this one,' providing a proof of lineage; and at other times: 'he who was thus justified ruled well.'

And so that the argument might appear more convincing, it is said he was deemed worthy even of angels, to whom, because of his divine infinity and unseeability, he was invisible before that time, similarly to the 'only invisible God,' and to be hymned by them: 'glory to God in the highest and on earth peace, in men goodwill' (Luke 2:14); and it has been preached in all this and believed, that he who shone out unceasingly from the unspeakable light, and through philanthropy was ineffably begotten from the eternally virgin in later times, expressing all the Fatherly things in himself, has ascended.

english: Lord. Therefore, how or when could you be inserted into such clear, equal, and incomparable oracles of the Father? 28.n Concerning the bringing forth of all good by the Son and being 'sun of righteousness and healing' (Mal 4:2) and 'treasure of wisdom and knowledge' (Col 2:3) and 'light', and the believers becoming 'sons of light, not stumbling in him'.

28.1 For those having hymned about him differently, demonstrating to us his divinity and his perfect presiding over his own works, teach that he is the provider of every good and a light that is good-looking and good-making and an intellectual sun, by whom the eyes of the unerring and receptive souls are made brilliant by the light from himself, and leading them into an inward contemplation and making them see things which they had not previously seen through sin by themselves, or even making the whole complete man light-like, just as the sun makes the bodies in which it arises sun-like; and furthermore, that he also is an unexhaustible and all-sufficient healing and 'treasure of wisdom and knowledge'.

28.2 And those sincerely disposed toward him become sons of light just as they do concerning his Father, as sons of God the Father, just as Malachi proclaims: 'the sun of righteousness shall rise for you who fear my name, and healing in his wings' (Mal 4:2); 28.3 and Peter in the second epistle: 'until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts' (2 Pet 1:19); 28.4 and he was saying, I think, that the one from his second appearance is about to rise to the souls as a light and making everything held by darkness shine brightly; 28.5 and also elsewhere: 'and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you' (Luke 1:78); 28.6 33 And Zechariah prophesied: 'if there is anything good, of him, and if there is anything beautiful, it will be from him' (Zech 6:12). 28.7 And Paul to the Colossians about him said: 'in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden' (Col 2:3), but to the Romans: 'for he says', he says.

“The Scripture says: ‘Everyone believing upon it will not be ashamed’ (Rom 10:9). For there is no distinction of Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is of all, rich toward all who call upon him. For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved (Rom 10:12-13).”

What name do they call upon the Son, those not saying he is uncreated God or the Son consubstantial with the Father, but calling him the fine net, the savior of heaven and earth and sea? And John similarly says concerning him: “As you have light, believe into the light, so that you become sons of light” (John 8:12).

For after death, he says, there is no repentance, as David sings: “And in Hades, who will confess to you?” (Ps 16:10). And again from the Savior: “Having gone, announce to John what you see and hear: the blind see again, the lame walk, and the dead are raised, and the poor are evangelized; and blessed is he who is not scandalized in me” (Matt 11:4-6).

For what will he say concerning the erring ones and those who lead astray? Isaiah foretold: “My people, those blessing you lead you astray and trouble the path of your feet. But now the Lord will be established for judgment and will set the people for judgment. The Lord himself will come for judgment with the elders of the people and with his rulers. But you, what have you done to my vineyard?” (Isa 5:1-7).

And the Lord himself will come for judgment with the teachers and rulers, not as he himself is to be judged by another, but as one who will convict them, just as he speaks in another part: “Come, let us examine, says the Lord, what things have come to be from me to you and what things have come to be from you to me and to my servants” (Isa 43:26).

For he says “vineyard” regarding the world or the people, whom the heretical and Jewish interpreters made guilty through blasphemous teaching regarding the fire of Gehenna, while the rulers, not owning what belongs to him and having made use of the authority, wronged in various and diverse ways.
